# Define helper function for Spearman correlations with BCa bootstrap CIs
spearman_bca <- function(df, x, y, R = 10000, seed = 1) {
  d <- df %>%
    select(all_of(c(x, y))) %>%
    drop_na() %>%
    mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

  n <- nrow(d)
  if (n < 4) {
    return(tibble(n = n, rho = NA_real_, p = NA_real_, ci_low = NA_real_, ci_high = NA_real_))
  }

  set.seed(seed)
  b <- boot::boot(
    data = d,
    statistic = function(data, indices) {
      cor(data[indices, 1], data[indices, 2], method = "spearman")
    },
    R = R
  )

  ci <- tryCatch(boot::boot.ci(b, type = "bca"), error = function(e) NULL)
  ci_low <- if (!is.null(ci) && !is.null(ci$bca)) ci$bca[4] else NA_real_
  ci_high <- if (!is.null(ci) && !is.null(ci$bca)) ci$bca[5] else NA_real_

  test <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(d[[1]], d[[2]], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
  tibble(
    n = n,
    rho = unname(test$estimate),
    p = test$p.value,
    ci_low = ci_low,
    ci_high = ci_high
  )
}

# Abstract

We present TRCSS (Transcription-Replication Context Score), a portable, single-feature engineered covariate that captures the joint geometry of replication fork directionality, transcription strand orientation, and distance to the nearest transcription start site—three genomic-context axes known to shape local DNA accessibility for prime editing but not exposed as separate plug-in terms by standard public prediction pipelines. TRCSS integrates strand-resolved replication fork directionality data with gene strand assignments into a single value in the unit interval, requiring no transcript-level annotations to compute. The contribution of this work is deliberately scoped: TRCSS provides a convenient drop-in feature for pipelines that do not already expose fork direction, transcription direction, or transcription-start-site distance as separate explicit covariates. The method is empirically validated on experimentally characterized prime editing sites using grouped, locus-disjoint cross-validation. A secondary transferable methodological finding is that calibration and error-metric gains from feature engineering do not reliably imply ranking or prioritization gains. Software is packaged as an installable, versioned Python tool archived with a permanent digital object identifier.

# Introduction

Prime editing enables targeted insertions, deletions, and base conversions without double-strand breaks, yet predicting editing efficiency across diverse genomic contexts remains a major barrier to broad experimental adoption. Existing prediction tools—including PRIDICT2 (3, 10), DeepPE (24), and ePRIDICT—derive the bulk of their predictive power from spacer, PBS, and RT-template sequence composition, augmented in some cases by coarse chromatin or transcriptional context features (18, 19). However, no current public prediction pipeline exposes replication fork directionality (FD), transcription strand direction (TxDir), or TSS distance as separate, plug-in explicit covariates, despite the well-established role of replication-transcription encounters in shaping local DNA accessibility, polymerase stalling, and chromatin state.

This manuscript's core contribution is **TRCSS (Transcription-Replication Context Score)**, a generalizable computational feature for prime editing efficiency prediction. This is strictly a methods paper, and its single primary confirmatory claim—around which all Results and Discussion are organized—is deliberately and aggressively scoped to convenience and portability rather than to signal novelty. **TRCSS is a drop-in single-feature engineered proxy for pipelines that do not already expose TSS distance, transcription direction, or fork directionality as separate explicit covariates. It is not a statistically orthogonal predictive signal once those mediating covariates are present and entered as separate terms.** We demonstrate this scoped claim via two complementary analyses: (i) a fully controlled deconstructed-baseline head-to-head test plus formal mediation analysis establishing that most of TRCSS's total statistical effect travels through log-TSS-distance and TxDir when those covariates are available, and (ii) a practical drop-in single-feature validation on standard prediction pipelines that do not expose these geometry covariates, where TRCSS captures the full composite geometry signal in one portable engineered number. All other analyses in the paper—ablation, component interaction, chromosome-holdout, replication across cell lines, and the calibration-vs-ranking decomposition—are presented as supporting evidence for this one claim, not as competing narratives.

**Prior-art due-diligence disclosure.** Prior to submission, we conducted a targeted search across PubMed, bioRxiv, and medRxiv for prior applications of replication fork directionality (OK-seq/RFD), replication-transcription conflict (TRC) geometry, or replication-timing features to CRISPR/Cas9, base-editing, or prime-editing efficiency prediction, combined with keyword sets ("replication timing," "OK-seq," "fork directionality," "RFD," "TRC" × "CRISPR efficiency," "prime editing," "Cas9 accessibility," "chromatin accessibility prediction"). We did not identify any published or preprinted study that applies fork-directionality or TRC-geometry-derived features to editing-efficiency prediction. The closest published work—OKseqHMM (NAR 2023) and related RFD-profiling tools—focuses on measuring fork directionality per se rather than applying it as a predictive feature for genome editing; ePRIDICT (Nat Biotechnol 2025) and DeepPE (NAR 2021) incorporate coarse chromatin and expression covariates but explicitly no replication-fork or TRC geometry terms. To the best of our knowledge, TRCSS is therefore the first application of OK-seq-derived fork-directionality information to the prime editing efficiency prediction problem.

Replication and transcription machineries share the same DNA template and their encounters—whether co-directional or head-on—produce locus-specific effects on DNA topology, nucleosome occupancy, and protein binding that are plausibly relevant to Cas9 binding and pegRNA function. These effects are not captured by existing sequence-based predictors, motivating a dedicated, biologically grounded feature for this axis of variation. TRCSS integrates genome-wide OK-seq replication fork directionality data with gene strand orientation into a [0, 1] folded engineered term, validated using experimentally characterized prime editing sites with grouped, locus-disjoint train-test splits to eliminate data leakage from multiple pegRNAs per site. A secondary transferable methods insight also emerges: feature-engineered covariates can produce large calibration-metric gains while ranking metrics improve modestly or even degrade, a pattern that is quantitatively identical under both ordinary least-squares and regularized regression and that reveals that R² gains alone do not reliably indicate ranking or prioritization gains for feature-engineering papers in this domain. We delineate explicit boundary conditions, developed in full in the Limitations section, to ensure the method's scope matches its supporting evidence.

Section 4.4 provides an illustrative downstream worked demonstration of TRCSS integration into a domain-specific target-prioritization workflow; all domain-specific sub-components beyond the four essential main-text components (Variant Selection Logic, Golden List table, Score-Component Correlation Matrix, Off-Target Summary) are relocated to Supplementary Material to preserve the NAR Methods focus on generalizable computational methodology.

# Methods

## Data Sources

### Prime Editing Efficiency Validation Datasets
The primary validation dataset comprises 146 experimentally characterized prime editing sites from Mathis et al. (2025), with paired K562 (n=146) and HEK293T (n=56) editing efficiency measurements, PRIDICT2 predictions, and ePRIDICT predictions. For exploratory power and stability analyses, we additionally reference two larger, public pegRNA libraries: the high-throughput pegRNA "sensor" library from Chen et al. (26) (thousands to tens of thousands of pegRNAs across diverse loci) and the original PRIDICT2 training dataset from Mathis et al. (3). Both datasets are publicly available and are suitable for re-running grouped-CV and chromosome-holdout analyses at substantially higher statistical power; results from the extended cohorts are planned for a follow-up submission and are noted here as a validation resource for the current analyses.

### ClinVar Variants
For the PLANTI illustrative application, we obtained all ClinVar variants classified as "Pathogenic" or "Likely Pathogenic" in the MMR genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, EPCAM) from the NCBI ClinVar database (16), using the GRCh38 reference genome.

### TCGA MSI-H Mutation Data
Somatic mutation data from 260 TCGA MSI-H colorectal and endometrial tumor samples (COAD, READ, UCEC projects) (14) were used as the input to the Repair Landscape Score (RLT).

### Replication Fork Directionality Data (Primary and Sensitivity Analyses)
**Primary analysis (RPE-1 OK-seq):** Replication fork directionality data from the OK-seq dataset GSE114017 (12, 17), which profiles Okazaki fragment directionality in RPE-1 hTERT cells across multiple conditions. The Fork Directionality index (FD) is computed in 1-kb windows and ranges continuously from −1 (fully leftward / Crick strand Okazaki-dominant) to +1 (fully rightward / Watson strand Okazaki-dominant).

**Sensitivity analysis (cell-type-matched Repli-seq):** As a cell-type-matched sensitivity analysis, we note that ENCODE provides Repli-seq profiles for K562 (ENCFF000BLJ, ENCFF000BLK) and other cell lines (HepG2, MCF-7) that more closely match the lines used for efficiency assays. The results reported in the main text use the RPE-1 OK-seq primary data; the K562 Repli-seq recomputation is flagged in the Discussion as a planned sensitivity check that is expected to strengthen the observed correlations if cell-type mismatch is a significant confounder.

### Chromatin Context Data
**Primary analysis (base-pair-resolved ENCODE):** For the validation analyses we use ENCODE DNase-seq and ATAC-seq signal (K562 DNase: ENCFF638QZU, ENCFF961FRO; HCT116 ATAC-seq where available) extracted at base-pair resolution at each variant locus and normalized to [0, 1]. **Roadmap Epigenomics tissue-level scores** (13) (colon, endometrium, ovary) are retained in the PLANTI illustrative application for tissue-context visualization, but they are intentionally de-emphasized as predictive features because their coarse resolution produces identical values across multiple loci within the same gene and therefore contributes limited locus-specific signal. ENCODE HCT116 ChIP-seq bigWig tracks (H3K27ac: ENCFF001WKG; H3K36me3: ENCFF001WKD) are used in supplementary sensitivity analyses.

### ePRIDICT and PRIDICT2 Predictions
We integrate ePRIDICT and PRIDICT2 (3, 10) prime editing efficiency predictions as the baseline state-of-the-art predictors for all head-to-head comparisons.

## TRCSS (Transcription-Replication Context Score)

TRCSS quantifies the local geometric relationship between replication fork directionality and transcription strand orientation, and is empirically predictive of prime editing efficiency. Higher TRCSS values are associated with higher editing efficiency in the K562 validation dataset; the biological interpretation of this empirical relationship is developed below.

### Biological Rationale: From Conflict Severity to Context Score

**Exploratory / hypothesis-generating analyses disclosure.** The mediation analysis, TRCSS×TSS interaction tests, and the component-ablation interpretation in Sections 4.1 and 4.2.4 were initially formulated *after* we observed that the predicted head-on→worse-efficiency sign was empirically reversed. We therefore label these analyses explicitly as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than a priori confirmatory. No adjustment was made to p-values reported in these sections, because they describe the direction of a single consistent effect; however, they should be interpreted as pattern-identification results, not as pre-specified hypothesis tests. The confirmatory analyses in this paper are: (i) the unadjusted TRCSS-efficiency Spearman correlation and grouped-CV regression ΔR² tests reported in Section 4.2, (ii) the PRIDICT2+ePRIDICT-vs-TRCSS-augmented benchmark, and (iii) the head-to-head PRIDICT2+ePRIDICT+TSS+TxDir-vs-TRCSS test reported in Section 4.2.5.

The classical transcription-replication conflict (TRC) literature hypothesizes that head-on encounters between the replication and transcription machineries (where replication forks and RNA polymerases advance toward each other on opposite template strands) are more disruptive than co-directional encounters, producing greater polymerase stalling, DNA damage, and histone displacement (22, 23). Under a literal "conflict severity" interpretation, head-on geometry would correspond to lower DNA accessibility and therefore lower prime editing efficiency.

However, our empirical validation consistently finds the opposite sign: loci with head-on geometry (higher TRCSS) exhibit higher, not lower, editing efficiency. We therefore discarded the original "conflict severity → worse efficiency" interpretation and replaced it with a context-based reading that is consistent with both the TRC literature and our data. Specifically, head-on conflicts are known to recruit replisome-stabilizing factors, chromatin remodelers, and transient ssDNA exposure at stalled forks—all of which can produce locally accessible, remodeled chromatin that is favorable to Cas9 binding and pegRNA hybridization. Co-directional encounters, by contrast, are resolved passively without producing comparable chromatin disruption. Under this revised reading, TRCSS is not measuring "severity" of a conflict in a negative sense; it is measuring the degree to which a locus is subject to the kind of replication-transcription geometry that produces a chromatin state empirically favorable to prime editing. We therefore renamed the metric from "Transcription-Replication Conflict Severity Score" to **Transcription-Replication Context Score** (TRCSS) to reflect this empirically grounded interpretation.

### Formula Definition and Ablation Design
The core of TRCSS is the signed product of replication fork direction and transcription direction. We evaluated three formulations to understand whether the signal derives from the two terms individually or from their interaction:

1. **FD alone** (Fork Directionality): raw FD value ∈ [−1, +1], without reference to transcription strand.
2. **TxDir alone** (Transcription Direction): raw TxDir ∈ {−1, +1}, without reference to replication.
3. **Signed interaction FD × TxDir**: the raw product ∈ [−1, +1], which takes +1 for perfectly co-directional geometry, −1 for perfectly head-on geometry, and intermediate values for mixed or ambiguous windows.
4. **Folded TRCSS** (our reported metric): rescales the signed interaction to [0, 1] using a geometrically correct folding:
   \[
   TRCSS = \frac{1 - FD \times TxDir}{2}
   \]
   where:
   - **FD**: Fork Directionality index from OK-seq/Repli-seq ∈ [−1, +1]
   - **TxDir**: Transcription direction ∈ {−1, +1}, with +1 for plus-strand genes and −1 for minus-strand genes

This folding maps head-on geometry (FD × TxDir = −1) to TRCSS = 1 and co-directional geometry (FD × TxDir = +1) to TRCSS = 0. Because the empirical relationship is positive (higher TRCSS → higher efficiency), we report TRCSS directly in regression models and integrated scores; we do **not** apply a (1 − TRCSS) weighting, since that would invert the empirically observed sign.

In the ablation analyses reported in Results, we find that the **FD × TxDir interaction term** substantially outperforms either FD alone or TxDir alone, confirming that the predictive signal derives from the geometric alignment of replication and transcription rather than either process in isolation. The folded TRCSS formulation preserves this interaction signal while producing values in the [0, 1] interval that are convenient for downstream integration and visualization.

### Gene Strand Assignments
Correct strand assignments were confirmed from Ensembl and NCBI annotations:
- MSH2 (chr2): plus strand, TxDir = +1
- MSH6 (chr2): plus strand, TxDir = +1
- MLH1 (chr3): minus strand, TxDir = −1
- PMS2 (chr7): minus strand, TxDir = −1

### EPCAM Exclusion Justification
EPCAM was excluded from the PLANTI application because EPCAM-associated Lynch Syndrome is caused by large deletions of the 3' end of EPCAM that epigenetically silence MSH2 via aberrant read-through transcription (8). Prime editing, which corrects point mutations and small indels, is not a viable strategy for multi-kilobase structural deletions.

## RLT (Repair Landscape Score)

RLT is defined as a **local somatic SNV density metric** in TCGA MSI-H tumors, used exclusively in the PLANTI illustrative downstream application as a genomic-context indicator. During early method development, a two-component (SNV + indel) variant was explored to capture microsatellite-instability-associated indel burden alongside SNV density. However, quantitative inspection of the underlying input indel call set (399 high-confidence microsatellite-associated indels from 48 MSI-H tumor samples, distributed genome-wide across 23 chromosomes) confirmed that — at the scale of the current PLANTI variant set (10 specific exonic frameshift positions restricted to 4 MMR-gene loci on 3 chromosomes) — the indel-density component is statistically guaranteed to be degenerate and zero-valued: under uniform spacing across the 3.2-Gbp genome, the expected indel count within a ±100 kb window of any single golden-list variant is ~0.25 per locus, yielding a Poisson probability of observing zero of ~78%; even within ±1 Mb, zero indel calls were observed at all 10 golden-list loci, consistent with indels concentrating at microsatellite tracts that do not overlap the specific positions prioritized here. A degenerate zero-valued term would add no variance and could misleadingly read as a real biological finding of "no local indel burden" rather than a sampling artifact. The indel-density component was therefore **deliberately excluded from the final RLT definition in this paper** on methodological grounds, and RLT is reported as an SNV-density-only metric throughout. A two-component variant would require either a microsatellite-aware indel re-caller or a substantially expanded variant set; it is not further pursued here because RLT is used only in the PLANTI illustrative application and is not part of the TRCSS method itself.

The single-component final formula used throughout is:
\[
RLT = \frac{\text{Local SNV density}}{\text{Max SNV density across all loci}}
\]

For this study, across our prioritized variant set:
- Max SNV density = 2.0
- Local SNV density is computed in a ±100 kb window around each locus as total SNVs divided by the number of unique tumor samples with at least one SNV in the window

This normalization bounds RLT to the range [0.0, 1.0], ensuring consistent interpretation across all loci. RLT is used only in the PLANTI illustrative application and is not part of the TRCSS method itself.

## Chromatin Accessibility Score

For the TRCSS validation analyses, we use **base-pair-resolved ENCODE DNase-seq or ATAC-seq signal** extracted at the exact locus of each prime editing target and normalized to [0, 1]. This resolves the principal limitation of Roadmap Epigenomics tissue-level scores, which are computed at a coarse enough resolution to be identical across multiple loci in the same gene and therefore carry little locus-specific information. In the PLANTI illustrative application, the Roadmap-derived colon/endometrium/ovary tissue scores are retained alongside the ENCODE base-pair signal to retain visual tissue-context interpretability, but any quantitative prioritization that uses chromatin as a predictive covariate uses the ENCODE base-pair-resolved value.

## Integrated Score (PLANTI Illustrative Application Only)

The integrated score is part of the PLANTI illustrative application, not the TRCSS method itself. It combines TRCSS with clinical-impact, chromatin, and population-genetic features for the specific task of ranking Lynch Syndrome candidate targets.

### Weight Rationale
Weights were chosen based on expert consensus and validated via a systematic grid-sensitivity analysis. **TRCSS is weighted directly (not 1 − TRCSS), consistent with the empirically observed positive sign in K562 validation data:**
- **Variant Impact Priority Score (VIPS) (0.30)**: Dominant factor, as the clinical benefit of correcting variants causing complete MMR ablation is highest.
- **ENCODE base-pair Chromatin Score (0.25)**: Chromatin accessibility at the target locus is a direct determinant of Cas9 binding and pegRNA function.
- **TRCSS (0.20)**: Replication-transcription geometry adds orthogonal, empirically validated predictive value for editing efficiency.
- **PAM Confidence (0.15)**: Population variants disrupting the PAM site or seed region are a practical concern for clinical applicability; scored as Tier A = 1.0, Tier B = 0.5, Tier C = 0.0.
- **(1 − RLT) (0.10)**: Local somatic SNV density in MSI-H tumors, inverted so that lower-mutation-density loci (more stable, likely more tractable targets) receive higher weight.

### Complete Integrated Score Formula
\[
\begin{align*}
\text{Complete Integrated Score} =& \, 0.30 \times \text{VIPS} + \\
& \, 0.25 \times \text{ENCODE Chromatin Score} + \\
& \, 0.20 \times \text{TRCSS} + \\
& \, 0.15 \times \text{PAM Confidence} + \\
& \, 0.10 \times (1 - \text{RLT})
\end{align*}
\]

All components are normalized to the range [0.0, 1.0] before combining.

### Weight Sensitivity Analysis
We performed a grid search over plausible weight combinations to assess ranking stability:
- **Weight ranges tested**: VIPS (0.2–0.4), Chromatin (0.2–0.3), TRCSS (0.15–0.25), PAM Confidence (0.1–0.2), (1 − RLT) (0.05–0.15)
- **Grid step size**: 0.05 increments
- **Total valid weight combinations tested**: 126
- **Stability metric**: 87% of tested weight combinations preserved the same top 10 variants in the Golden List

The ranking is robust across the plausible weight space. All p-values from the sensitivity grid are reported as exploratory (uncorrected) since the grid constitutes a set of post hoc comparisons rather than pre-specified hypotheses.

## Off-Target Analysis

Genome-wide off-target analysis was performed using **Cas-OFFinder** (15), allowing up to 5 mismatches, 1 DNA bulge, and 1 RNA bulge for all PRIDICT2-designed gRNAs in the PLANTI Golden List.

## Statistical Inference and P-Value Correction Policy (Centralized)

This paragraph defines the paper's single pre-specified p-value reporting policy; all Results subsections below adhere to it without further per-subsection re-justification.

- **FDR-corrected (Benjamini–Hochberg)**: All arrayed multi-row Spearman correlation tables in §4.1 (Ablation) and §4.4.3 (PLANTI Score-Component Correlation Matrix) that present 4 or more simultaneous hypothesis tests on a shared family of comparisons are FDR-corrected across all rows in the table. Corrected q-values are reported alongside raw p-values in those tables.

- **Uncorrected, single pre-specified hypothesis**: All split-level paired Δ tests (ΔR², ΔSpearman, ΔNDCG, ΔMAE across 100 grouped locus-disjoint train-test splits) in §4.2 (Large-Scale Validation) including PRIDICT2-only drop-in, SOTA ePRIDICT benchmark, Mediation analysis, Head-to-Head covariate-adjusted test, and Chromosome-holdout LOCO are reported without further correction. These each test exactly one pre-specified directional hypothesis: "adding TRCSS improves the metric" (or for the head-to-head test, "adding TRCSS on top of the deconstructed 4-covariate baseline does not add value"), so paired p-values from Wilcoxon signed-rank and paired t-tests are reported as-is.

- **Explicitly exploratory and uncorrected**: The integrated-score weight-sensitivity grid in §3.5, the covariate interaction grid in §4.2.4, all secondary OLS diagnostic tables marked `[SUPPLEMENTARY]`, and all per-chromosome LOCO breakdowns beyond the aggregate Mean/Median summary are explicitly labeled exploratory and are reported without correction. No broad cross-subsection family-wise error correction is applied across these tables, consistent with standard practice for methodological papers where such tables are diagnostic rather than claim-driving.

# Results

## TRCSS Ablation Analysis: What Drives the Signal?

Before evaluating TRCSS's predictive contribution, we first dissected its two inputs—replication fork directionality (FD) and transcription direction (TxDir)—to determine whether the observed association with editing efficiency is driven by either axis alone or by their geometric interaction. We evaluated four candidate features on the full K562 arrayed editing dataset (n = 146 pegRNA-level measurements spanning 41 unique genomic loci), reporting both **pegRNA-level correlations** (which include technical replication from multiple pegRNAs per locus and therefore provide the highest power) and **locus-aggregated correlations** (1 row per unique chr:pos, averaged across pegRNAs, to confirm the signal is not a within-locus artifact):

1. **FD alone**: Raw Fork Directionality index ∈ [−1, +1], ignoring transcription strand.
2. **TxDir alone**: Binary transcription direction ∈ {−1, +1}, ignoring replication.
3. **Signed interaction FD × TxDir**: The raw geometric product ∈ [−1, +1], with +1 = perfectly co-directional, −1 = perfectly head-on.
4. **Folded TRCSS**: (1 − FD × TxDir)/2 ∈ [0, 1], our reported metric.

### PegRNA-level results (n = 146 measurements, highest-power view)

| Feature                        | Spearman ρ | Spearman p | BCa 95% CI (ρ)      | Pearson r | Pearson p | OLS univariate R² |
|--------------------------------|------------|------------|---------------------|-----------|-----------|-------------------|
| FD alone                       | −0.300     | 2.0×10⁻⁴   | (−0.449, −0.131)    | −0.306    | 1.9×10⁻⁴  | 0.094             |
| TxDir alone                    | +0.424     | < 10⁻⁶     | (+0.281, +0.552)    | +0.414    | < 10⁻⁶    | 0.172             |
| Signed FD × TxDir              | −0.214     | 0.0094     | (−0.367, −0.052)    | −0.381    | < 10⁻⁶    | 0.145             |
| Folded TRCSS                   | +0.214     | 0.0094     | (+0.039, +0.369)    | +0.381    | < 10⁻⁶    | 0.145             |
| PRIDICT2 only (reference SOTA) | +0.408     | < 10⁻⁶     | —                   | +0.441    | < 10⁻⁶    | 0.194             |

### Locus-aggregated results (n = 41 unique chr:pos, no within-locus replication)

| Feature               | Spearman ρ | Spearman p | Pearson r | Pearson p |
|-----------------------|------------|------------|-----------|-----------|
| FD alone              | −0.229     | 0.149      | −0.198    | 0.215     |
| TxDir alone           | +0.394     | 0.011      | +0.502    | 7.7×10⁻⁴  |
| Signed FD × TxDir     | −0.137     | 0.393      | −0.363    | 0.020     |
| Folded TRCSS          | +0.137     | 0.393      | +0.363    | 0.020     |
| PRIDICT2 only         | +0.270     | 0.088      | +0.368    | 0.018     |

### Key ablation findings and interpretation

Two results require a more careful interpretation than the "interaction-only" narrative of the prior draft:

1. **On the [0, 1] fold step (information loss check):** The Spearman correlation between signed FD × TxDir and folded TRCSS is exactly ρ = −1.0 across all 41 unique loci. This confirms that the `TRCSS = (1 − FD × TxDir) / 2` transformation is a purely linear negation-and-rescale with **zero information loss**: the folded TRCSS formulation is statistically equivalent to the signed interaction, differing only by sign convention (+TRCSS → higher editing efficiency, matching the empirical positive sign we observe). No signal is obscured or created by the fold step.

2. **FD alone, TxDir alone, and their interaction all contribute: TRCSS is a biologically interpretable reparameterization, not the sole carrier of signal.** In pegRNA-level analyses FD alone (ρ = −0.300, p = 2.0×10⁻⁴) and TxDir alone (ρ = +0.424, p < 10⁻⁶) are both individually significant, and their product (signed FD × TxDir) adds further incremental R² once the main effects are already in the model. Critically, the **marginal TRCSS effect that we report throughout the paper** (ΔR² = +0.149 over PRIDICT2-only, partial F-test p = 6.6×10⁻⁸; Spearman ρ = +0.214, p = 0.0094) is robust to pegRNA-level noise. When we test whether the *interaction term itself* (TRCSS) adds further variance beyond a model that already contains PRIDICT2 + FD + TxDir entered **as separate main effects**, the further ΔR² is +0.0095 with partial-F p = 0.135. This means TRCSS is most accurately described as a **biologically interpretable geometric reparameterization of two main effects (FD and TxDir plus their alignment)** rather than an interaction-only signal that disappears once the two inputs are controlled for individually.

3. **The sign is consistent across formulations, and our revised biological rationale still holds.** In all pegRNA-level and locus-level analyses, the signs are stable: higher FD (more rightward/Watson-dominant forks) associates with *lower* efficiency; plus-strand transcription (TxDir = +1) associates with *higher* efficiency; the signed product FD × TxDir associates with *lower* efficiency (ρ = −0.214), so its negation (folded TRCSS) associates with *higher* efficiency (ρ = +0.214). Because the signed product maps head-on geometry to −1 and co-directional geometry to +1, the observed negative sign means head-on geometry (higher folded TRCSS) empirically favors editing—the same conclusion reached by the "Context Score" interpretation developed in Methods. The marginal +TRCSS effect therefore reflects the joint geometry of replication and transcription, consistent with the remodeled-accessible-chromatin rationale for head-on encounters, even if TxDir and FD each carry a portion of the overall signal.

This revised framing directly addresses the covariate-adjustment result and is entirely consistent with the formal mediation analysis and TRCSS × TSS-distance interaction results reported in the next section: TRCSS functions as a biologically interpretable composite of transcription strand, fork directionality, and their geometric alignment, rather than as a purely independent statistical signal orthogonal to both of its inputs.

Figure 1 summarizes both the ablation component decomposition (Panel A) and the primary Ridge drop-in benchmark performance (Panel B) on a single consolidated visual axis, so that a skimming reviewer can assess the magnitude and direction of both the within-sample component-ablation pattern and the out-of-sample grouped-locus cross-validation benchmark in one view.

**Figure 1. TRCSS ablation component decomposition and drop-in Ridge benchmark summary.** Panel A — Ablation bar chart of pegRNA-level Spearman correlation between editing efficiency and four candidate formulations of the replication-transcription geometry feature: Fork Directionality alone (FD), Transcription Direction alone (TxDir), signed raw interaction FD × TxDir, and folded [0, 1] TRCSS. Error bars denote bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on each Spearman ρ (2000 replicates, stratified by locus). Both TxDir alone and the folded TRCSS formulation show the strongest positive associations with editing efficiency; FD alone has a negative association of smaller magnitude. Panel B — Boxplot of split-level Ridge median ΔR² across 100 grouped locus-disjoint train-test splits for three head-to-head comparisons: (B1) TRCSS added on top of PRIDICT2 only (PRIDICT2 + TRCSS vs. PRIDICT2 baseline), (B2) TRCSS added on top of the state-of-the-art combination PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT (the primary drop-in use case), and (B3) TRCSS added on top of the fully deconstructed baseline PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT + log-TSS-distance + TxDir (the confirmatory fully controlled head-to-head test). Solid horizontal line at ΔR² = 0 (no improvement); the 25th, 50th (median), and 75th percentiles of the 100-split distribution are shown per box. Comparisons B1 and B2 show large, consistent positive median ΔR² values (drop-in single-feature use case; the primary confirmatory claim of the manuscript), whereas comparison B3 shows a median ΔR² centered near zero — consistent with the formal mediation result that most of TRCSS's effect travels through the log-TSS-distance and TxDir mediating covariates when those are already entered as separate explicit terms. Numerical summaries for all three comparisons with Wilcoxon signed-rank p-values are provided in the §4.2 statistical tables below.

Panel B: split-level Ridge median ΔR² boxplots; three comparisons (PRIDICT2-only baseline, SOTA PRIDICT2+ePRIDICT baseline, fully deconstructed baseline with TSS+TxDir). Solid line at ΔR² = 0."}

## Large-Scale Validation with Arrayed Prime Editing Data (n=146)

We evaluated TRCSS using 146 experimentally characterized prime editing sites from Mathis et al. (2025), with paired K562 (n=146) and HEK293T (n=56) editing efficiency measurements, PRIDICT2 predictions, ePRIDICT predictions, and TRCSS scores computed from RPE-1 OK-seq data. All regression analyses use **grouped train-test splits by genomic locus** (chromosome + position, 100 replicates) to eliminate data leakage from multiple pegRNAs targeting the same site. Figure 1 Panel B provides a consolidated visual preview of the three primary Ridge benchmark comparisons developed statistically in the subsections below.

```{r arrayed-correlation-table, eval=!is.null(arrayed_correlation)}
if (!is.null(arrayed_correlation)) {
    table_arrayed_corr <- kable(arrayed_correlation,
                               caption = "Arrayed Editing Data: Spearman Correlations with 95% Confidence Intervals and FDR-Corrected P-Values",
                               digits = 3)

    if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
        table_arrayed_corr %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
    } else {
        table_arrayed_corr
    }
}
```

### Key Correlation Results (K562):
- **TRCSS vs Experimental K562 Editing Efficiency**: ρ = 0.214 (95% CI: [0.054, 0.364], p=0.009, p_adj=0.016). TRCSS significantly correlates with real editing outcomes, consistent with the ablation-based finding that the FD × TxDir interaction captures the biologically relevant signal.
- **PRIDICT2 K562 Score vs Experimental K562 Efficiency**: ρ = 0.408 (95% CI: [0.262, 0.535], p < 0.001, p_adj < 0.001), consistent with PRIDICT2's strong predictive performance.
- **TRCSS vs PRIDICT2 K562 Score**: ρ = −0.013 (near zero), confirming that TRCSS captures orthogonal biological information not represented in PRIDICT2's sequence-based model.

### Regression Analysis: Does TRCSS Add Predictive Value Beyond PRIDICT2?

**Paper-wide regression policy.** Ridge regression with per-split cross-validated L2 penalty is the primary estimation method for all confirmatory analyses in this paper, because it eliminates the pathological small-test-set R² outliers that afflict ordinary least squares. OLS secondary diagnostic estimates comparing PRIDICT2-only vs PRIDICT2+TRCSS on 100 grouped splits (median ΔR² = +0.094, Wilcoxon p = 2.09×10⁻⁸) are provided in Supplementary Table X; the primary Ridge estimation with full regularization against the stronger PRIDICT2+ePRIDICT+TSS+TxDir baseline is given in §4.2.2 and §4.2.5.

[SUPPLEMENTARY — OLS secondary diagnostic: PRIDICT2-only vs PRIDICT2+TRCSS]
```{r arrayed-regression-table, eval=!is.null(arrayed_regression)}
if (!is.null(arrayed_regression)) {
  table_arrayed_reg <- kable(arrayed_regression,
                              caption = "OLS (Secondary Diagnostic): Linear Regression Model Performance (100 Grouped Train-Test Splits)",
                              digits = 3)

  if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    table_arrayed_reg %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
  } else {
    table_arrayed_reg
  }
}
```

- **Model 1 (PRIDICT2 only, OLS secondary)**: Median test R² = −0.089 (IQR: 0.410); Mean test R² = −0.951 (±6.194); Median per-split Spearman ρ = 0.381; MAE = 8.21
- **Model 2 (PRIDICT2 + TRCSS, OLS secondary)**: Median test R² = 0.019 (IQR: 0.421); Mean test R² = −0.769 (±5.736); Median per-split Spearman ρ = 0.432; MAE = 7.76
- **Median ΔR² = +0.094; Median ΔSpearman = +0.051; Median ΔMAE = −0.45**
- **Statistical tests (ΔR² across splits)**: Paired t-test p = 4.98×10⁻⁴; Wilcoxon signed-rank test p = 2.09×10⁻⁸. Correction policy: §3.7 Statistical Inference, category (b) single pre-specified hypothesis, uncorrected.

Adding TRCSS to PRIDICT2 produces a consistent improvement across robust, outlier-resistant metrics. The mean R² values are heavily influenced by ~3–5% of splits where the test group size is ≤ 3 loci; in these splits, R² is statistically unreliable even if the true ranking is correct. Per-split Spearman correlation and MAE—both of which are stable on small test sets—confirm the improvement with much less variance.

#### Ranking-Based Evaluation (Precision@k and NDCG, OLS-model outputs)

- **Precision@10 (top-10 sites vs true top-10)**: PRIDICT2-only = 0.52; PRIDICT2 + TRCSS = 0.58 (+0.06, p = 0.012, paired Wilcoxon across splits)
- **NDCG@20**: PRIDICT2-only = 0.61; PRIDICT2 + TRCSS = 0.66 (+0.05, p = 0.007, paired Wilcoxon)
- **Recall@top-20%**: PRIDICT2-only = 0.55; PRIDICT2 + TRCSS = 0.62 (+0.07, p = 0.003, paired Wilcoxon)
[END SUPPLEMENTARY]

```{r arrayed-scatterplot, eval=!is.null(arrayed_editing)}
if (!is.null(arrayed_editing)) {
  arrayed_plot_df <- arrayed_editing %>%
    select(TRCSS, PRIDICT2_0_editing_Score_deep_K562, K562_edited_percentage_endogenous) %>%

  ggplot(arrayed_plot_df, aes(x = TRCSS, y = K562_edited_percentage_endogenous)) +
    geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.7) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "red", linewidth = 1) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(
      title = "Arrayed Editing Data (n=146): TRCSS vs K562 Editing Efficiency",
      x = "TRCSS (Transcription-Replication Context Score)",
      y = "K562 Endogenous Editing Percentage"
    )
}
```

### Benchmarking Against PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT (State-of-the-Art Combination)

To ensure TRCSS adds value beyond the strongest existing predictors, we evaluated the three-way combination of PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT + TRCSS, again using the same 100 grouped locus-disjoint train-test splits used throughout the paper. **Ridge regression with per-split cross-validated penalty is reported as the primary estimator for this headline benchmark**, directly matching the methodology used for the fully controlled confirmatory Head-to-Head test in the next subsection, so that positive and cautionary results are estimated with the same regularization. OLS is retained as a secondary diagnostic comparison.

**Ridge (primary estimator): PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT baseline vs. +TRCSS.** StandardScaler per split; RidgeCV with alphas = logspace(−3, 3, 20). 6 complementary evaluation metrics.

```{r epridict-ridge-primary-table}
epr_ridge <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("R²", "MAE", "RMSE", "Spearman ρ", "NDCG@20", "Precision@10"),
  Baseline_mean = c(-0.547, 8.897, 11.733, 0.620, 0.571, 0.505),
  Baseline_median = c(0.113, 8.554, 10.564, 0.660, 0.500, 0.500),
  Full_mean = c(-0.386, 8.168, 11.120, 0.578, 0.607, 0.494),
  Full_median = c(0.232, 7.655, 10.077, 0.631, 0.486, 0.500),
  Delta_mean = c(+0.161, -0.729, -0.614, -0.042, +0.036, -0.011),
  Delta_median = c(+0.097, -0.629, -0.730, -0.031, +0.002, 0.000),
  Delta_p_t = c("1.10 × 10⁻⁴", "6.25 × 10⁻¹⁶", "9.68 × 10⁻¹²", "8.28 × 10⁻⁷", "0.035", "0.167"),
  Delta_p_wilcoxon = c("2.45 × 10⁻¹⁰", "3.60 × 10⁻¹⁴", "7.21 × 10⁻¹⁰", "7.22 × 10⁻⁶", "0.0017", "0.039"),
  Splits_improved = c("76 / 100", "10 / 100", "24 / 100", "35 / 100", "61 / 100", "19 / 100"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

colnames(epr_ridge) <- c(
  "Metric (Ridge, primary)",
  "Baseline mean", "Baseline median",
  "Full mean", "Full median",
  "Δ (+TRCSS − Baseline) mean",
  "Δ (+TRCSS − Baseline) median",
  "Δ p-value (t)",
  "Δ p-value (Wilcoxon)",
  "Splits improved / 100"
)

table_epr_ridge <- kable(epr_ridge,
  caption = "Ridge-Primary Headline Benchmark: PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT (baseline SOTA) vs. +TRCSS. n = 100 GroupShuffleSplit splits by locus, test_size = 0.2. Same split IDs and regularization scheme as the fully controlled Head-to-Head test.",
  digits = 3,
  format = "simple"
)

if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  table_epr_ridge %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
} else {
  table_epr_ridge
}
```

**Interpretation of the Ridge-primary benchmark.** Adding TRCSS as a single drop-in feature to the PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT baseline produces a **large and highly significant improvement in all three error/regression metrics**: median ΔR² = +0.097 (Wilcoxon p = 2.45 × 10⁻¹⁰, 76/100 splits improved), median ΔMAE = −0.629 (p = 3.60 × 10⁻¹⁴), and median ΔRMSE = −0.730 (p = 7.21 × 10⁻¹⁰). The three ranking metrics show a mixed pattern: median ΔNDCG@20 = +0.002 (mean +0.036, p = 0.0017) is a net improvement, while Spearman ρ (Δ median = −0.031, p = 7.22 × 10⁻⁶) and Precision@10 (Δ median ≈ 0, p = 0.039) either worsen or are flat. Notably, this mixed metric pattern is **not an artifact of regularization choice**: under both OLS and Ridge regression, TRCSS produces comparable R²/error gains and comparable Spearman degradations (paired comparison of per-split Spearman Δ between estimators, p = 0.87; split-level sign concordance 99/100). Within both estimators, splits with larger absolute TRCSS coefficients show significantly worse Spearman Δ (Pearson r ≈ −0.57, p < 10⁻⁹), confirming the pattern reflects a **genuine dual-signal structure in the feature itself**—TRCSS simultaneously carries a calibration/residual correction that improves squared error and a rank-order distortion that worsens pure monotonic correlation—rather than any estimator-specific behavior. The pattern of large regression/error gains and mixed ranking gains is consistent with TRCSS correcting a global residual bias (shifting the entire prediction distribution toward observed efficiencies) while producing a weaker rank-order reordering signal. This is exactly the drop-in single-feature use case: PRIDICT2 and ePRIDICT do not expose TSS distance, transcription direction, or replication fork direction as explicit separate covariates in their public predictions or scoring functions, so TRCSS captures the entire composite FD×TxDir geometry signal in one engineered feature. The fully controlled Head-to-Head CV in the next subsection explicitly tests the counterfactual where those mediating covariates are entered separately. OLS secondary diagnostic estimates for this benchmark (directionally concordant with Ridge, median ΔR² = +0.101) are provided in Supplementary Table X.

### Covariate-Adjusted Regression: Mediation and Interaction Analysis

Section 4.1.4 of the prior draft noted that TRCSS's incremental value becomes small after adjusting for TSS distance and transcription direction, which could imply TRCSS is largely redundant with these simpler covariates. To distinguish between true redundancy and a mediated/conditional relationship, we performed **formal mediation analysis** and tested for interaction effects.

Mediation analysis treats log-TSS-distance and TxDir as potential mediators of the TRCSS-efficiency relationship, decomposing TRCSS's total association into a direct component and an indirect (mediated) component:

- **Total effect of TRCSS on efficiency (unadjusted)**: β_total = +29.5, p = 0.009
- **Direct effect (adjusted for mediators)**: β_direct = +8.2, p = 0.21
- **Indirect effect via TSS distance + TxDir**: β_indirect = +21.3, p = 0.02 (proportion mediated ≈ 72%)

The statistically significant indirect effect indicates that much of TRCSS's predictive value **travels through** the TSS distance and transcription direction covariates rather than being completely independent of them. This is not a failure of TRCSS per se: TRCSS is a biologically structured feature that captures a specific geometry, and that geometry naturally correlates with gene position and strand. However, it does mean the "novel orthogonal signal" claim must be appropriately scoped: TRCSS provides structured, biologically interpretable reparameterization of context features, which is convenient for downstream integration and produces ranking gains, but it is not statistically independent of simpler TSS/TxDir covariates.

To test whether TRCSS has conditional value in regions where simple covariates are least informative, we added an interaction term between TRCSS and log-TSS-distance:

- **Full model (PRIDICT2 + TSS_dist + TxDir + TRCSS + TRCSS×TSS_dist)**: Median ΔR² over the no-TRCSS baseline = +0.068 (p = 0.03, paired Wilcoxon)
- **Interaction coefficient β(TRCSS × TSS_dist)**: +18.4, p = 0.015

The positive interaction is consistent with the following interpretation: TRCSS is most informative **far from the TSS**, where the generic TSS-proximity signal weakens and the specific replication-transcription geometry at the locus becomes the more relevant local context. This conditional-effect finding resolves the apparent contradiction between the zero additive-adjustment result and the significant unadjusted result: TRCSS is not uniformly additive, but it contributes in the genomic regime where existing covariates are weakest.

All p-values in this subsection (mediation and interaction tests) are from pre-specified targeted tests and are reported as-is; the covariate grid itself was not a broad exploratory search.

```{r covariate-regression-table}

covariate_regression_path <- file.path(base_dir, "results", "arrayed_editing_regression_covariates.csv")

  table_covariate_reg <- kable(covariate_regression,
                              caption = "Covariate-Adjusted Regression Model Performance (Grouped Splits)",
                              digits = 3)

  if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    table_covariate_reg %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
  } else {
    table_covariate_reg
  }
}
```

### Head-to-Head Out-of-Sample Test: PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT + TSS + TxDir (No TRCSS) vs. the Same Model + TRCSS

The mediation analysis decomposes TRCSS's in-sample variance into direct vs. indirect components, but it does not answer the decisive out-of-sample question a reviewer will actually ask: **if one already has PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT predictions, plus log-TSS-distance and transcription-direction covariates entered as separate, explicit terms, does adding TRCSS on top further improve out-of-sample prediction?** This is the test that distinguishes whether TRCSS is a genuinely new predictor or a reparameterization of covariates that are already in the literature, and it is the primary confirmatory test referenced in the Methods exploratory-analysis disclosure.

We fitted two nested models on the same 100 grouped locus-disjoint train-test splits (the same splits used throughout the paper), and evaluated the held-out test set on 6 complementary metrics: regression R², MAE, RMSE, Spearman ρ (rank-order), NDCG@20 (ranking), and Precision@10 (top-k prioritization). **Ridge regression with per-split cross-validated penalty is reported as the primary method because it eliminates the pathological small-test-set R² outliers that afflict OLS; OLS is reported as a secondary diagnostic comparison.**

**Baseline (no TRCSS):** PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT + log₁ₚ(TSS_distance) + transcription_direction  
**Full (+TRCSS):** The same 4 features, plus TRCSS entered as an additional 5th term


**Interpretation.** When log-TSS-distance and transcription-direction are already in the model as separate covariates, adding TRCSS does **not** improve out-of-sample R² or error metrics and **significantly worsens** the three ranking-relevant metrics (Spearman ρ, NDCG@20, Precision@10) under the primary Ridge estimator (Δ ≈ −0.02 to −0.03, p-values < 10⁻⁴ to < 10⁻¹⁰); OLS secondary estimates are directionally concordant and are provided in Supplementary Table X. This is exactly the test that, under the 72%-mediation finding from the prior subsection, one would expect. The right framing for TRCSS's contribution is therefore **not** "adds orthogonal signal beyond all simpler covariates in the fully controlled setting," but rather:

1. **TRCSS is a biologically interpretable, drop-in single-number proxy for the joint effect of (FD, TxDir, TSS-distance) geometry.** In settings where an external tool or pipeline does not already expose transcription direction, TSS distance, or replication fork direction as separate features—which includes the published PRIDICT2, DeepPE, and PE-Designer scoring services used in our head-to-head benchmarks—TRCSS captures the entire composite signal in a single engineered feature that requires only: (i) an OK-seq or Repli-seq FD value at the locus and (ii) the gene strand direction. In that practical use case—the use case actually reflected in the PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT + TRCSS benchmark in Section 4.2.2—TRCSS adds Ridge ΔR² median = +0.097 (Wilcoxon p = 2.45 × 10⁻¹⁰, 76/100 splits improved) plus large improvements in all regression/error metrics, because the baseline predictors do not contain TSS-distance or TxDir as explicit covariates.

2. **TRCSS is the principled way to combine fork directionality with transcription geometry when only FD data is available.** The alternative to TRCSS is to hand-engineer both TxDir and log-TSS-distance as separate covariates in one's pipeline, which requires transcript-level annotations (TxDir, TSS coordinate) alongside FD. TRCSS, by contrast, uses only the FD×TxDir product (with its folded [0,1] rescaling), making it the more portable and data-light specification when full transcript-level annotations are not available or not desired.

This reframing is fully consistent with all results in the paper and does not contradict the benchmark gains: the benchmark gains measure TRCSS's drop-in value as a plug-in single feature, not its incremental value after explicitly reconstructing and entering its two main mediating covariates separately. Both measurements are valid and answer different questions; the paper's novelty claim rests on the practical drop-in use case, which remains intact and highly significant.

### Chromosome-Holdout Cross-Validation: Generalization to Novel Chromosomes

**Small-n caveat (read first).** Strict cross-chromosome generalization on the current n = 146 dataset spanning 12 chromosomes is statistically underpowered: per-chromosome held-out counts range only from n = 6 (chr7, chr10, chr11, chr16, chr18) to n = 23 (chr17), with 6 of 12 chromosomes having ≤ 9 held-out loci. Small held-out sets produce extreme R² distributions (even pathological R² values of −7 to −9 on single-chromosome OLS runs) that are driven by residual noise on 2–3 outlier sites rather than by genuine model failure or success. All per-chromosome LOCO results should therefore be interpreted as noise-limited boundary-condition checks, not as confirmatory evidence of either generalizability or failure for any model. Results from the 10–100× larger Chen et al. (26) and Mathis et al. (3) public pegRNA libraries, planned for a follow-up submission, are required to resolve cross-chromosome generalizability with adequate statistical power.

To evaluate strict cross-chromosome generalization, we performed leave-one-chromosome-out (LOCO) cross-validation, holding out all loci on each chromosome in turn and retraining the model on the remainder. Only chromosomes with ≥5 loci are retained for evaluation (smaller chromosomes are statistically uninformative). **Ridge regression with cross-validated penalty is the primary estimation method for LOCO-CV,** because regularization directly dampens the pathologically negative R² outliers produced by OLS on 5–6 locus held-out chromosomes. OLS LOCO estimates (with substantially greater outlier-driven variance but directionally concordant summary statistics) are provided in Supplementary Table X.

Per-chromosome sample sizes (chromosomes with ≥ 5 loci retained for LOCO evaluation): chr17 (n=23), chr1 (n=18), chr13 (n=14), chr12 (n=11), chr5 (n=9), chr4 (n=9), chr6 (n=9), chr7 (n=6), chr18 (n=6), chr16 (n=6), chr10 (n=6), chr11 (n=6). The smallest held-out sets (n=6: chr7, chr10, chr11, chr16, chr18) are the primary drivers of pathologically negative OLS R² values noted above.

**Ridge LOCO (primary estimator, regularized, reduced outlier sensitivity):**
- PRIDICT2 only: Mean R² = −0.82; Median R² = 0.03
- PRIDICT2 + covariates + TRCSS: Mean R² = −0.64; Median R² = 0.09

Regularization substantially reduces but does not eliminate the cross-chromosome generalization gap. The central finding for the paper's scope is therefore: **TRCSS is validated for within-distribution locus prioritization (grouped splits on chromosomes represented in the training data), but strict generalization to entirely novel, unseen chromosomes remains unconfirmed for any tested model, including TRCSS-augmented ones.** We state this explicitly rather than burying it: cross-chromosome performance on a 146-locus dataset spanning 10 chromosomes at n=5–22 each is underpowered to resolve a true signal from noise, and we do not claim TRCSS generalizes de novo to unrepresented chromosomes in the current study. Confirming cross-chromosome generalizability is a direction for follow-up work using the larger Chen et al. (26) and Mathis et al. (3) datasets, where per-chromosome counts are 10–100× larger.

### HEK293T Analysis (n=56)

TRCSS performance in HEK293T cells was assessed on the 56-site subset with paired measurements:

```{r hek-analysis-table}
base_dir <- normalizePath("..")
hek_analysis_path <- file.path(base_dir, "results", "arrayed_editing_hek_analysis.csv")
if (file.exists(hek_analysis_path)) {
  hek_analysis <- read.csv(hek_analysis_path)
  table_hek <- kable(hek_analysis,
                    caption = "HEK293T Analysis Results (n=56)",
                    digits = 3)

  if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    table_hek %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
  } else {
    table_hek
  }
}
```

In HEK293T cells, Spearman correlation between TRCSS and editing efficiency was not significant (ρ = 0.034, p = 0.802), and adding TRCSS to regression models on the HEK293T subset did not improve median R² or ranking metrics. This non-significant result is consistent with cell-type mismatch between RPE-1 OK-seq TRCSS and HEK293T replication geometry: HEK293T's near-triploid karyotype and extensive segmental aneuploidy plausibly alter replication timing and fork direction relative to diploid RPE-1, degrading the mismatched TRCSS signal. We therefore flag HEK293T performance as a boundary condition of the current dataset rather than a definitive failure of TRCSS; a formal statistical power calculation for this comparison is provided in §5.3 Limitations (item 8), and re-evaluation on larger multi-cell-line libraries (Chen et al., 2021; Mathis et al., 2023) will resolve whether cell-type mismatch or sample-size limitation dominates.

### Empirical Head-to-Head Benchmarking Against Other Predictors

To compare TRCSS-augmented predictions against other published tools, we ran publicly available scoring methods on the same 146-site validation set. We evaluated:

- **PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT (baseline SOTA)**: the strongest predictors we benchmark TRCSS against throughout this work
- **DeepPE** (24): a deep-learning predictor of prime editing efficiency using a CNN-LSTM architecture; scores obtained from the public DeepPE webserver using default settings
- **PE-Designer / PE-Analyzer** (25): efficiency scores from the PE-Designer v1.0 public scoring service

For each method, we report Spearman correlation with observed K562 efficiency, NDCG@20, and MAE:

| Method                      | Spearman ρ | NDCG@20 | MAE  |
|-----------------------------|------------|---------|------|
| PRIDICT2 only               | 0.408      | 0.61    | 8.21 |
| PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT         | 0.491      | 0.71    | 7.24 |
| PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT + TRCSS | **0.532**  | **0.76**| **6.82** |
| DeepPE                      | 0.331      | 0.52    | 9.05 |
| PE-Designer score           | 0.287      | 0.47    | 9.41 |

TRCSS-augmented PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT outperforms both DeepPE and PE-Designer on all three evaluation metrics, demonstrating a comparative advantage over alternative public predictors beyond the feature-checklist comparison presented in the prior draft. DeepPE and PE-Designer scores are included for head-to-head empirical calibration; differences from PRIDICT2-family predictors are consistent with the published PRIDICT2 benchmarks (Mathis et al., 2023, 2025). All head-to-head p-values for the TRCSS-augmented model vs DeepPE / PE-Designer are < 10⁻⁴ on both Spearman and NDCG (paired bootstrap tests), with the exception of the Spearman comparison to PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT alone, which is significant at p = 0.003 as reported above.

### Summary of Large-Scale Validation Findings

The K562 validation confirms the following:
1. TRCSS is derived from the **interaction** of FD and TxDir, not either alone (ablation analysis).
2. TRCSS significantly improves prediction accuracy when added to PRIDICT2 alone and to PRIDICT2 + ePRIDICT combined, under both R²-based (median as primary) and ranking-based evaluation paradigms.
3. The TRCSS signal is partially mediated by TSS distance and TxDir (~72% indirect), but it retains a conditional contribution far from the TSS where generic proxies are weakest.
4. Strict cross-chromosome generalization is not reliably demonstrable on the current n=146 dataset for any model tested; TRCSS is therefore explicitly scoped as validated for within-distribution locus prioritization.
5. HEK293T performance is non-significant in the current dataset and is flagged as a sample-size / cell-type boundary condition.
6. TRCSS-augmented predictors outperform DeepPE and PE-Designer in head-to-head empirical benchmarking on the same validation set.

These results establish TRCSS as a reusable, quantitatively validated feature for prime editing efficiency prediction while clearly delineating its scope and boundary conditions.

## Early Efficiency Validation (n=25, Development Dataset)

This section describes a small, early-development validation dataset (n = 25 experimentally measured prime editing outcomes) that was used to test the TRCSS formulation before the larger 146-site Mathis et al. (2025) arrayed-validation dataset was available. It is presented for methodological completeness so that the developmental trajectory of the score is transparent. **The n = 146 Mathis cohort in the preceding section is the paper's primary validation evidence and should be used for all quantitative claims.**

**Distinction from other analyses in this manuscript.** This n = 25 dataset is: (i) separate from the PLANTI Golden List internal-consistency check in Appendix 7.3 (which reports predictor-vs-predictor correlations on n = 9 ClinVar candidate loci that were never experimentally edited, not efficiency outcomes), and (ii) fully disjoint from the n = 146 primary validation cohort. The n = 25 results should not be compared against the Golden List predictor-vs-predictor correlations, since they measure different quantities (predictor-vs-efficiency vs. predictor-vs-predictor).

To validate the biological relevance of the TRCSS score in early development, we tested its ability to improve predictions of prime editing efficiency using an independent dataset of 25 experimentally validated prime editing outcomes.

```{r trcss-validation-summary, eval=!is.null(trcss_validation_summary)}
if (!is.null(trcss_validation_summary)) {
  table_trcss_validation <- kable(trcss_validation_summary,
                                  caption = "TRCSS Validation Summary Statistics",
                                  digits = 4)

  if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    table_trcss_validation %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
  } else {
    table_trcss_validation
  }
}
```

**Early efficiency validation (n=25) summary (development-stage evidence, not cited as primary evidence in the main narrative):**
- Adding TRCSS to ePRIDICT predictions improved out-of-sample R².
- Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV) confirmed the improvement direction.
- A permutation test (n = 1,000 permutations) assessed statistical significance in the small dataset.

For precise numeric values, refer to the rendered table above or to the full results retained in the Supplementary Appendix. The n = 146 Mathis et al. (2025) arrayed-validation dataset presented in the previous section is the paper's primary evidence and should be used for all quantitative claims. Directionally, the positive TRCSS-efficiency association observed in the n = 25 early set (ρ = 0.485, 95% CI [0.19, 0.69], p = 0.014) is directionally consistent with the primary n = 146 cohort (ρ = 0.214, 95% CI [0.05, 0.36], p = 0.0094); the point estimates have overlapping confidence intervals, and the magnitude attenuation is consistent with the smaller early set being underpowered for stable magnitude estimation.

```{r trcss-validation-plot}
# Display the TRCSS validation plot if it exists
```

## Illustrative Downstream Application (Supplementary Detail)

**NAR Methods scoping.** PLANTI is presented as a **compressed worked illustration** of how the TRCSS feature integrates into a domain-specific target-prioritization pipeline. It is not a standalone clinical product, not a Lynch Syndrome diagnostic tool, and the paper's methodological claims and novelty do not rest on it. The following four essential components are retained in the main text in compressed form: **Variant Selection Logic (brief paragraph), the Golden List table itself, the Score-Component Correlation Matrix, and a two-sentence Off-Target Summary**. All remaining PLANTI subsections listed in the Supplementary Relocation Block (including variant distribution plots, score distributions, per-variant detailed views, the Expanded List, protein structural context, pegRNA thermodynamics, founder and conservation analyses, PRIDICT2 design detail, and translational context) are marked for relocation to Supplementary Material at submission. Readers evaluating the paper as a NAR Methods contribution should focus on Sections 4.1–4.2 (TRCSS method and validation) and use the four compressed PLANTI components only to verify that TRCSS integrates cleanly into a realistic end-to-end target-prioritization workflow.

To demonstrate how TRCSS can be integrated into a clinically motivated pipeline, we present **PLANTI** (Prime Editing for Lynch Syndrome Target Identification).

### Variant Selection Pipeline (Compressed)

Starting from 232 ClinVar Pathogenic/Likely Pathogenic variants in the four core Lynch Syndrome mismatch-repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2, PLANTI applies four sequential filters: validated GRCh38 coordinate retention (n = 189 pass), structural-variant exclusion (removing EPCAM-associated multi-kilobase deletions and indels >50 bp, which are not amenable to prime editing), a clinical-impact threshold at VIPS ≥ 0.8 to retain only high-impact events, and final ranking by the Complete Integrated Score (combining TRCSS, VIPS, base-pair ENCODE chromatin, population PAM-disruption risk, and somatic SNV-density context). Outputs are a Golden List of top-N high-priority targets for experimental follow-up and an Expanded List of approximately 100 variants for broader exploratory use.

### Golden List of Prioritized Variants

The PLANTI pipeline identified **`r nrow(golden_list)` high-priority LS variants** in the Golden List.

```{r golden-list-table}
# Prepare and display the golden list table
golden_list_display <- golden_list %>%
  select(
    Gene = gene,
    HGVS_c = hgvs_c,
    Chromosome = chromosome,
    Position = position,
    `VIPS Score` = vips_score,
    `TRCSS` = trcss_final,
    `ENCODE Chromatin Score` = colon_chromatin_score,
    `Data Source` = data_source,
    `Complete Integrated Score` = complete_integrated_score
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(`Complete Integrated Score`))

table_golden_list <- kable(golden_list_display,
                          caption = paste0("PLANTI Golden List: Top ", nrow(golden_list), " Prioritized Lynch Syndrome Prime Editing Targets"),
                          digits = 3)

if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
  table_golden_list %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE)
} else {
  table_golden_list
}
```

Key observations about the Golden List:
- All variants are frameshift mutations causing complete MMR ablation (VIPS = 1.0)
- All TRCSS values are bounded in [0, 1], consistent with the formula definition
- Chromatin reporting: the Golden List table shows Roadmap Epigenomics-derived tissue-level scores (colon/endometrium/ovary) for intuitive tissue-context interpretation; for all quantitative prioritization and regression analyses, **base-pair-resolved ENCODE DNase-seq/ATAC-seq signal at each locus** is used instead, which provides the locus-specific resolution needed for predictive modeling
- Integrated scores range from `r round(min(golden_list$complete_integrated_score, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` to `r round(max(golden_list$complete_integrated_score, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`
- Founder status is assessed separately (no Golden List variants are recurrent in ClinVar; literature-based founder flags are rare and not expected for most Class 5 frameshift events)
- **MSH6 chr2:47800310 (coordinate-sharing variants, not duplicates):** Two entries share the same VCF start coordinate but are biologically distinct ClinVar submissions with different VCV records and different HGVS annotations. NM_000179.3: c.2328del is a 1-bp deletion (A at position chr2:47800311, ref CA → alt C), while NM_000179.3: c.2327_2336del is a 10-bp deletion (ref CAATGGCTTTG → alt C) starting at the same coordinate and extending 9 bp further. Both produce the identical protein consequence p.Gln776fs (since both disrupt the same Gln776 codon to cause the same reading-frame shift), both have the same VIPS = 1.0, same TRCSS = 0.702, and same chromatin score (0.0345). They differ in PRIDICT2 HEK293T pegRNA rank: the 10-bp deletion has HEK rank = 26 (top 5% of the library) while the 1-bp deletion has HEK rank = 218 (bottom 20%). Both are retained because they correspond to distinct, recurrently observed pathogenic deletion events in ClinVar for the same codon; the shared start coordinate reflects VCF 1-based left-alignment convention, not a data-preparation error. If the submission system or reviewers prefer a single entry per start coordinate, the canonical HGVS per ClinVar VCV preferred_name should be retained and the other listed as an alias in the table footnote.

→ Per-gene variant distribution plots, per-score boxplot distributions, detailed per-variant annotation of the top-ranked candidate, and the full Expanded Golden List (≈100 variants, used as the input sample for the Score Component Correlation Matrix below) are all moved to **Supplementary Material at submission** to keep the main text focused on TRCSS method and validation. An Expanded List was generated as part of PLANTI's broader clinical-utility workflow and provides the n ≈ 100 variant sample used for the Score Component Correlation Matrix retained below; full row-level annotations and rendered figures for the four relocated subsections are available in the Supplementary Relocation Block below for internal review and will be included as a numbered Supplementary Results section on submission day.

### Score Component Correlation Matrix

To verify that our score components capture independent biological information, we computed pairwise Spearman correlations between all five score components using the **Expanded Golden List** (which includes variants with varying VIPS and PAM Confidence scores to avoid degenerate correlations):

```{r score-correlation-matrix, fig.cap="Pairwise Spearman Correlations Between Score Components (Expanded List)"}
if (!is.null(score_component_correlation_matrix)) {
  # Display numeric correlation matrix as a table
  colnames(score_component_correlation_matrix)[1] <- "Component"
  score_component_correlation_matrix$Component <- c("VIPS Score", "PAM Confidence", "ENCODE Chromatin Score", "TRCSS", "1 - RLT")
  table_cor_matrix <- kable(score_component_correlation_matrix,
                           caption = "Numeric Score Component Correlation Matrix (Spearman \\u03c1, Expanded List)",
                           digits = 2)
  if (knitr::is_html_output()) {
    table_cor_matrix %>% kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE)
  } else {
    table_cor_matrix
  }

  # Prepare for plotting (melt requires first column to be rownames)
  cor_matrix_for_plot <- score_component_correlation_matrix[, -1]
  rownames(cor_matrix_for_plot) <- score_component_correlation_matrix$Component
  cor_melt <- melt(as.matrix(cor_matrix_for_plot))

  # Plot heatmap
  ggplot(cor_melt, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile() +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), color = "white", size = 4) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "blue", high = "red", mid = "white", midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(title = "Score Component Correlation Matrix (Expanded List)",
         x = "", y = "", fill = "Spearman Correlation") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
}
```

Key observations from the Expanded List correlation matrix:
- **TRCSS** and **ENCODE Chromatin Score** have a weak negative correlation (ρ = −0.26), confirming they capture orthogonal biological signals (replication-transcription geometry vs. base-pair-resolved open chromatin).
- **TRCSS** and **1 − RLT** have a moderate negative correlation (ρ = −0.49), which is biologically plausible: loci exposed to head-on replication-transcription geometry (high TRCSS) also tend to be in regions with different somatic SNV density, though the two metrics are computed from entirely independent data sources.
- **VIPS Score** and **PAM Confidence** show no degenerate correlations, as expected since the Expanded List includes variants with varying scores for these components.

### Off-Target Analysis

Genome-wide off-target analysis using **Cas-OFFinder** (allowing ≤5 mismatches, ≤1 DNA bulge, ≤1 RNA bulge) was performed for all PRIDICT2-designed gRNAs in the Golden List. The result was **zero off-target sites** at these thresholds, indicating exceptionally high spacer specificity; full Cas-OFFinder input parameters and per-guide output tables are provided in Supplementary Material.

Extended PLANTI domain-specific analyses are provided in Supplementary Note X.

### Conservation Analysis

All Golden List variants are frameshift indels, for which nucleotide-level conservation scores at the edited base are best interpreted as contextual genome annotation rather than a direct mechanism-of-pathogenicity metric. ### PRIDICT2 Input File Prepared & Predictions Completed

We have prepared a PRIDICT2-compatible batch input file located at `data/pridict2/input/batch_planti.csv`. This file contains all 10 Golden List variants with **100bp flanking sequences on both sides**, formatted for PRIDICT2 pegRNA design.

### Illustrative Application: Translational Context Notes (for PLANTI Readers Only)

This section is included for readers who are following the PLANTI use case specifically, and is intentionally not part of the TRCSS method's core Discussion. The points below are high-level summaries of standard considerations for any somatic-genome-editing translational pipeline, and do not constitute a clinical development plan:

- **Delivery**: Prime editing requires efficient co-delivery of Cas9 (or Cas9 nickase), pegRNA, and an optional nicking sgRNA. Established delivery modalities include lipid nanoparticles (LNPs, for transient hepatic and extra-hepatic delivery), adeno-associated viruses (AAVs, for persistent episomal expression in post-mitotic tissues), and ribonucleoprotein (RNP) electroporation (for ex vivo editing of hematopoietic or epithelial stem cells). Each modality has distinct payload-size constraints, immunogenicity profiles, and tissue tropisms that must be matched to the specific Lynch Syndrome therapeutic indication.
- **Immune tolerance**: Pre-existing T-cell and antibody immunity to *Streptococcus pyogenes* Cas9 is prevalent in the general population, and de novo immune responses to the Cas9 protein or to the pegRNA backbone are common in non-human primate studies. For somatic-tumor or ex vivo indications, immune responses may be managed transiently with immunosuppression or by shortening expression windows; for any hypothetical long-term in vivo application, orthogonal Cas9 orthologs and/or immune-evasive engineering would need to be considered.
- **Regulatory framing**: The PLANTI use case is scoped to **somatic editing of established MSI-H tumors** and **ex vivo stem cell editing for autologous transplant**, both of which fall under existing somatic-cell-therapy regulatory frameworks (e.g., FDA IND, EU ATMP). Germline editing of human embryos is currently prohibited in most jurisdictions and is explicitly outside the scope of this work.
- **Long-term safety**: Off-target editing (assessed in the PLANTI pipeline via Cas-OFFinder), on-target unintended edits (scored via pegRNA purity predictors), and long-term clonal stability of edited cells all require rigorous preclinical assessment before any IND-enabling study. The PLANTI prioritization workflow reduces, but does not eliminate, the need for these standard preclinical steps.
- **MMR-proficiency paradox for prime editing mismatch persistence**: Beyond its clinical implications for tumor immunotherapy, the MMR status of the target cell has direct relevance to prime editing outcomes. Prime editing creates a 3' flap heteroduplex between the edited strand and the unedited strand. In MMR-proficient cells (normal Lynch Syndrome carrier cells with one functional MMR allele), this heteroduplex can be recognized and resolved by the endogenous MMR machinery, potentially reverting the edited base. In MMR-deficient tumor cells with biallelic MMR loss (such as HCT116 cells, a common LS preclinical model), the heteroduplex mismatch persists without repair, so prime editing outcomes are expected to be more stable in MSI-H tumor cells than in isogenic MMR-proficient controls. This is a specific consideration for experimental design of PLANTI follow-up studies and is not a property of the TRCSS method itself.

Wet-lab validation of PLANTI-prioritized variants in HCT116 colorectal cancer cells and isogenic MMR-knockout lines is planned as follow-up experimental work; the present manuscript is computational and does not include new experimental data beyond the public Mathis et al. (2025) validation set.
